Below is a draft essay. Revise it so that it reads as if a US grade 12 student wrote it in class for a timed writing test. Keep the position it argues and keep it at about 456 words. The file must contain only the revised essay.

A measurement tool compared the draft with essays that students wrote on other assignments. Use its report when you revise:

Tone check against human essay writing (456 words). Distance from the human centre: 0.65 (1.0 is typical for a human text).
- how unevenly charge is spread over sentences: 1.81 (1 = as if words were dealt at random); most human texts are between 0.62 and 1.66. Feeling is bunched into fewer sentences than in human writing of this kind.
- negative charge: 23.49 (dolors per 1,000 words); most human texts are between 2.68 and 22.41. The draft uses more negative words than people do here.
Inside the human range: positive charge; net charge; total charge, positive plus negative; words that carry charge; charge under a negation; charge after an intensifier such as 'very'; charge after a contrast word such as 'but'; net charge of the last fifth minus the text's mean.
These are ranges, not targets. Change wording only where the change also makes the text more specific or more honest.

Draft:

Learning From Home Should Be an Option

When my cousin broke her leg in tenth grade, she missed almost six weeks of school. Her teachers sent home packets, but nobody explained the chemistry, and she spent the rest of the year trying to catch up. If her school had let her join classes by video, she would have lost very little. I think students would benefit from being able to attend classes from home, as long as it is offered as a choice and not forced on everyone.

The clearest benefit is for students who cannot physically get to school. Illness, injuries, family emergencies, and bad weather all keep students out of the classroom, and every missed day makes the next one harder. A student with the flu may feel well enough by the third day to listen to a lesson, but not well enough to sit in a crowded room and spread it around. With a distance option, that student keeps up with the class and the other students stay healthy. Rural students gain even more. Some of them ride a bus for over an hour each way, which is two hours a day that could go toward homework, sleep, or a job.

Distance learning also helps students who do not work well in a traditional classroom. Some students have anxiety that makes a noisy building exhausting. Others are distracted by classmates or are bullied in the hallways. At home they can focus on the material itself. Recorded lessons add another advantage, because a student who did not understand a math problem the first time can replay the explanation instead of pretending to follow along.

There are real concerns, and I do not want to ignore them. Students at home can drift off, open another tab, or stop showing up at all. They also miss the social side of school, like lunch conversations, group projects, and sports. Not every family has fast internet or a quiet room, either. These problems are serious, but they are reasons to design the option carefully, not reasons to refuse it. Schools can require cameras during discussions, check in with online students weekly, lend out laptops and hotspots, and let students move back to the building if their grades fall.

Finally, learning online is a skill students will need later. Many colleges run courses online, and many jobs involve video meetings and managing your own time. Practicing that in high school, with teachers still watching closely, is safer than learning it alone at eighteen.

School in person will remain the best fit for most students. But for the sick, the distant, and the ones who struggle in a crowd, a seat at home is far better than an empty desk.
